KEY MESSAGE 1...As of 12:50 AM EST...High pressure is centered 
to the south of our region, with an upper shortwave passing to 
our north leading to just a few mid and high clouds across the 
region. Some of the more sheltered areas have seen temperatures 
drop into the upper 20s to low 30s, but areas where the wind has
remained light and areas of the Catskills that remain above the
low-level inversion are still in the 40s. Dry weather should 
continue through Sunday morning as sfc high pressure slides 
overhead tomorrow night and then off to our east Saturday 
afternoon. Upper ridging amplifying overhead will also help 
promote large- scale subsidence and dry weather. Highs will 
remain several degrees above normal into the weekend under the 
ridge. Nighttime lows will be seasonably cool tomorrow night, 
but trend above average Saturday night with increasing clouds 
ahead of our next weather system...

Sunday, multiple upper shortwaves will begin to phase over the upper 
Midwest, while an area of low pressure will be tracking up the east 
coast on the west side of the aforementioned upper ridge. This 
area of low pressure may take on tropical or subtropical 
characteristics (please see nhc.noaa.gov for more detail). 
Regardless of its classification, we are expecting to see an 
area of rain spread north late Sunday into Monday. Deep 
southerly flow will help advect a plume of anomalous moisture 
northwards ahead of the potential coastal low Sunday, with PWATs
climbing 2-3 std dev above normal per the latest NAEFS. This 
moisture will begin to interact with the mid- latitude forcing 
as it moves north. We will be near the right entrance region of 
an anticyclonically curved upper jet streak to our north. Given 
this, along with an upper trough to the west and some hints of a
sfc inverted trough ahead of the main area of low pressure, 
there are some signals for a predecessor rain event (PRE) ahead 
of the main coastal low. As the coastal low works its way 
northwards, low-level warm advection and mid-level fgen 
strengthen, providing additional forcing for ascent leading to 
additional rain. The heaviest rain is expected Sunday night into
Monday, tapering off Monday afternoon. 

The main point of forecast uncertainty is how far west the axis of 
heaviest rain will make it. This will depend on the track of the sfc 
low, which will be influenced by a few different factors. 
Cluster analysis shows that one of the main factors will be the 
east-west position and amplitude of the upper trough over the 
upper Midwest/southern Canada and the downstream ridge over the 
Northwest Atlantic. This will likely depend not only by the 
complex interaction/phasing of the various shortwaves over the 
center of the country, but also by whether latent heat release 
help to amplify the downstream ridge. The other factor will be 
how "wrapped up" the initial sfc low becomes as it forms along a
frontal boundary east of Florida. If the initial low is 
stronger and consolidates more of the vorticity associated with 
this frontal boundary, then the sfc low will be more likely to 
track further west towards the coast. If more of this vorticity
and moisture "escapes" to the east (similar to what the 00z GFS
showed), then a more disorganized storm with a track further 
east would become more likely. 

As far as rainfall amounts and impacts, there is fairly good 
agreement amongst the various ensemble clusters for a stripe of up 
to 2-3" of rain on the west side of the low track, but would not be 
surprised if some locally higher amounts are realized due to the 
overlap of strong forcing and anomalous moisture. If the sfc low 
track is a little more east (currently the more likely 
scenario), then this would keep the heaviest rain east of our 
region with little to no impacts. If the sfc low track is 
further west, closer to the coast (less likely at this time, but
still on the table), then some of the heavier rainfall amounts 
(up to 2-3") could get into the Mid Hudson Valley and/or 
Litchfield County. Some of the recent 18 and 00z guidance has 
trended a little further west with the low track (i.e. wetter 
solution), so will continue to monitor to see if this is the 
start of a larger trend, or just noise in the model guidance. 
Thanks to the recent stretch of dry weather, even 2- 3" of rain 
over 12-24 hrs is unlikely to cause significant hydro issues, 
although if we see more than this then ponding of water in 
urban/poor drainage areas and rises on local rivers and streams 
would be possible (mainly south and east of the Capital 
District). With some of the newer guidance nudging the heavier 
rainfall amounts further west, WPC has adjusted their marginal 
risk ERO north and west into our forecast area. The latest HEFS 
still show a less than 10% chance of any main stem rivers 
reaching minor flood stage.
